who: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT; ran in Dem primaries)
promise_or_claim_verbatim: “Medicare for All does not represent any new spending at all. Instead, it represents a rebalance of how our current dollars are spent.”
what_the_record_shows_raw_numbers: CBO Dec 2020 (5 single-payer options, year 2030): federal health subsidies rise from $2,820B (current law) to $4,333B–$5,816B, i.e. +$1,513B to +$2,996B in one year. Total national health spending changes by -$743B, -$650B, -$158B, -$42B, or +$290B depending on design (current law $6,631B). CMS NHE 2024 actual: $5,278.6B total; federal share $1,652.0B.
finding: Federal spending rises by $1.5T–$3.0T a year in every CBO option. The claim is accurate only in the narrower sense that total national health spending changes little, and falls in 4 of 5 options.
label: Rated misleading

promise_or_claim_verbatim: “Not one penny in middle-class tax increases.” (Medicare for All financing plan)
what_the_record_shows_raw_numbers: No CBO or JCT score of the Warren financing plan exists. CBO's generic analysis (Mar 2021): paying for new spending of 5% of GDP through labor taxes raises average labor tax rates from 17.7% to 23.9%–27.5% by 2030. CBO does not assess Warren's specific mix of an employer contribution, wealth tax and enforcement revenue.
finding: No official scoring either confirms or refutes it.
label: Unsupported

who: H.R. 40 sponsors (Reps. Conyers, then Jackson Lee; S. 40 Booker) / California proposals
promise_or_claim_verbatim: Reparations proposals: official cost record (no single campaign dollar promise rated)
what_the_record_shows_raw_numbers: CBO (May 17, 2021): H.R. 40 would cost $20 million over 2021–2026, for the study commission only. No federal agency has scored reparation payments themselves. The California Task Force final report (2023), ch. 17, gives economists' harm estimates, e.g. ~$228B (housing discrimination, 2020 dollars) and ~$70.66B per year (labor-market losses, 2019). These are loss estimates, not a budget score. California: SB 518 (2025, Ch. 586) created a Bureau for Descendants of American Slavery, subject to future appropriation. AB 7, AB 57, AB 62 and AB 742 (2025) were vetoed. SB 1403 and SB 1331 (2024) died. No state cash-payment program has been enacted.
finding: The only official federal cost figure is $20M, and it covers the commission, not payments. Any national dollar figure for payments has no CBO or JCT estimate behind it.
label: Record summary (Unsupported for any national payment price tag)

promise_or_claim_verbatim: “No one earning less than $400,000 a year will pay an additional penny in federal taxes.” (pledge, repeated in several forms)
what_the_record_shows_raw_numbers: The statute (P.L. 117-169) raised no individual income-tax rate. JCT #D-16-22 (Aug 10, 2022, Senate-passed IRA, selected provisions, mainly the 15% corporate minimum tax and the buyback excise) allocates part of those taxes to households. For CY2023 it estimates +$10.6B total for income categories under $200K (e.g., $50–75K +$1,222M; $100–200K +$6,833M) and +$8.7B for $200–500K. The table EXCLUDES the ACA subsidy extension and some credits that lower taxes for many of the same households.
finding: True for statutory rates. The official scorekeeper's distribution tables show some new corporate and excise tax borne indirectly by households under $400K, and they omit the offsetting credits.
label: Rated misleading

promise_or_claim_verbatim: “we're going to cut the deficit—I point out—by another $300 billion with the Inflation Reduction Act over the next decade.”
what_the_record_shows_raw_numbers: CBO cost estimate of the enacted law (Sep 7, 2022): deficit -$58.1B over 2022–2031, plus a non-scorable -$180.4B from IRS enforcement revenue, for about -$238.5B combined. The ~$300B figure matched the earlier Senate-bill framing (CBO Aug 3, 2022: -$90B before IRS revenue; revised down $11B on Aug 5).
finding: Right direction (CBO shows deficit reduction), but the $300B figure is about $61B above CBO's estimate for the law as signed.
label: Rated misleading

promise_or_claim_verbatim: Inflation Reduction Act would reduce inflation (bill title; administration messaging)
what_the_record_shows_raw_numbers: CBO letter (Aug 4, 2022): effect on inflation in calendar 2022 'negligible'; in 2023, between -0.1 and +0.1 percentage point.
finding: The official analysis found essentially no measurable inflation effect in the near term.
label: Rated misleading

promise_or_claim_verbatim: Cancel a minimum of $10,000 of federal student debt per borrower (2022 plan: up to $10,000; up to $20,000 for Pell recipients)
what_the_record_shows_raw_numbers: The Supreme Court (6–3) held the HEROES Act did not authorize the plan, so $0 was cancelled under it. Separately, ED reports $188.8B approved for about 5.3M borrowers through existing programs (PSLF, IDR, borrower defense, disability) across 33 actions (Jan 16, 2025).
finding: The across-the-board cancellation did not happen; the Supreme Court struck it down. Targeted relief of $188.8B for 5.3M borrowers did happen under other authorities.
label: Proven false (promise not delivered as stated; blocked by Court)

promise_or_claim_verbatim: “If you like your health care plan, you'll be able to keep your health care plan, period.”
what_the_record_shows_raw_numbers: The administration's own interim final rule (June 17, 2010) estimated that 39% (low), 51% (mid) and 69% (high) of all employer plans would lose grandfathered status by end of 2013. For individual-market policies it estimated 40%–67% per year. The CMS letter of Nov 14, 2013 acknowledged that issuers were cancelling policies and created a transitional policy.
finding: The government's own records projected, and then acknowledged, that many people could not keep their plans.
label: Proven false

promise_or_claim_verbatim: “Compelling Mexico to Pay for the Wall” (campaign position paper); “Mexico will pay for the wall”
what_the_record_shows_raw_numbers: U.S. appropriations for barrier: FY2018 $1,375M (P.L. 115-141 §230, barrier lines of the $1,571M), FY2019 $1,375M (P.L. 116-6 §230), FY2020 $1,375M (P.L. 116-93 §209). All came from U.S. Treasury funds. Additional DoD transfers were also U.S. funds. No appropriations or Treasury receipt record shows any payment from Mexico.
finding: U.S. taxpayers funded the wall. The record shows no payment from Mexico.
label: Proven false

promise_or_claim_verbatim: Get rid of the $19 trillion national debt “over a period of eight years.”
finding: The debt rose instead of falling.
label: Proven false

promise_or_claim_verbatim: “the country is making approximately $2 billion a day. ... And the number is probably 3½ billion dollars a day.” (tariffs; Cabinet meeting)
what_the_record_shows_raw_numbers: MTS customs duties: April 2025 $15.63B (~$0.52B/day). The highest month on record, Oct 2025, was $31.35B (~$1.01B/day). FY2025 total $194.9B (~$0.53B/day). After the Supreme Court's IEEPA ruling (Feb 20, 2026), net customs receipts were negative in May–Jul 2026 (-$0.04B, -$25.56B, -$8.55B) because of refunds.
finding: No month reached $2B per day, let alone $3.5B.
label: Proven false

promise_or_claim_verbatim: “I took in hundreds of billions of dollars from China and others—taxes on China—but we took in hundreds of billions of dollars a year from China”
what_the_record_shows_raw_numbers: Total customs duties from ALL countries: FY2018 $41.3B, FY2019 $70.8B, FY2020 $68.6B. By regulation (19 CFR 141.1(b)), duties are a debt of the U.S. importer, not of the exporting country.
finding: Yearly duties from every country combined were $41–71B, not hundreds of billions from China. U.S. importers, not China, pay them.
label: Proven false

who: Treasury Dept. (Sec. Steven Mnuchin) / Trump administration
promise_or_claim_verbatim: Tax plan would generate “$1.8 trillion of additional revenue ... over 10 years”, more than offsetting its ~$1.5T static cost (i.e., pays for itself)
what_the_record_shows_raw_numbers: JCT macro analysis of the TCJA conference agreement (Dec 22, 2017): conventional cost $1,456B (2018–2027). Growth feedback recovers about $451B, less $66B of added interest, for a net $385B, leaving the net cost at about $1,071B. CBO (Apr 2018, App. B) also projected large deficit increases from the law.
finding: The official scorekeepers found that growth recovers about one-quarter of the cost, not all of it.
label: Proven false

promise_or_claim_verbatim: “We're going to have insurance for everybody.” (ACA replacement)
what_the_record_shows_raw_numbers: CBO/JCT on the House-passed AHCA he backed (May 24, 2017): 23M more uninsured in 2026, deficit -$119B. Senate BCRA (June 2017): 22M more uninsured, deficit -$321B. Neither was enacted.
finding: The official score of the replacement he endorsed showed more uninsured, not coverage for everybody.
label: Proven false (per official score)

promise_or_claim_verbatim: “The One Big Beautiful Bill reduces deficits by over $2 trillion”
what_the_record_shows_raw_numbers: CBO (P.L. 119-21 as enacted): +$3.4T deficits 2025–2034 (revenues -$4.5T, spending -$1.1T); +$4.1T with interest; +$5.0T if the temporary provisions are made permanent. The White House counts against a 'current policy' baseline that assumes the 2017 cuts were already extended. CBO scored the Senate substitute against that baseline too (pub. 61533), but that does not produce a $2T cut.
finding: Under CBO's official current-law score, the law adds $3.4T.
label: Proven false (per CBO)
